  "old_string": "## Consequences (anticipated)",
  "new_string": "## Phase-1 decision record (2026-07-04 — the build, PR for #461)\n\nPulled forward to v1.1 W1 at cycle planning (2026-07-04): the second authenticator must land\nwhile Azure AD is still live as the reference validator (the Azure window closes ~2026-07-25),\notherwise the seam's one real impl can never be regression-checked against the new one.\n\n**As built:**\n\n- **Token format:** `dq_live_` + `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` (~256 bits of entropy).\n- **Hash-at-rest: SHA-256 (hex), not argon2/bcrypt — a deliberate deviation** from the\n  stub's credential bar, for verifier-shaped reasons:\n  - Slow KDFs exist to protect **low-entropy human passwords** from offline brute force. A\n    PAT is machine-generated with ~256 bits of entropy — preimage-resistant under plain\n    SHA-256; a KDF adds no security margin against guessing.\n  - PATs are verified on **every request** (not once per session). An argon2/bcrypt\n    verification costs ~50–300 ms by design — a per-request tax; SHA-256 is microseconds.\n  - bcrypt-style salted hashes cannot be **looked up by index** — verification would be an\n    O(n) scan over all keys. SHA-256 gives an O(1) unique-index lookup on `key_hash`.\n  - Same trade-off GitHub and GitLab ship for their PATs.\n- **Uniform 401:** unknown, revoked, and expired keys return byte-identical\n  `invalid_api_key` errors — no oracle to probe key state. Bad keys never fall through to\n  the Azure branch (a `dq_live_…` bearer is decided by the PAT branch alone), and in local\n  dev-bypass mode a bad PAT 401s rather than degrading to the bypass identity.\n- **Seam wiring, REST:** the Azure scheme moves to `auto_error=False`; `get_current_user`\n  tries the PAT branch first (disjoint by prefix — a PAT is never a valid JWT), then Azure,\n  else a standard 401. Service/route code is untouched — the seam held (ADR 0010 validated).\n- **Seam wiring, MCP:** a composite `TokenVerifier` (PAT by prefix, else the Azure\n  `JWTVerifier`) rather than fastmcp `MultiAuth` — both credentials are bearer strategies on\n  the one `Authorization` header, so a prefix branch inside one verifier is the whole\n  composition. The PAT-resolved user id rides a DataQ-internal claim into\n  `resolve_current_user`.\n- **Expiry:** default 90 days, max 365, **no non-expiring keys**. Revocation is a soft\n  `revoked_at` mark (row kept for audit); user delete cascades keys (owner-lifecycle bar).\n- **Surface:** `POST/GET /api/v1/me/api-keys`, `DELETE /api/v1/me/api-keys/{id}` —\n  self-service, show-once, list is metadata-only. Prefix-only logging.\n- **`last_used_at`** is throttled to one write per 60 s per key — audit signal without a\n  hot-path write amplification.\n- **Not in phase 1:** key down-scoping (read-only), the management UI (API-only for now),\n  and service-account principals (phase 2, unchanged).\n\nOpen questions carried: scope granularity, principal generalization, and where service\naccounts sit relative to the workspace-admin allowlist. The token-verification-cost question\nis answered by the indexed-SHA-256 design above (no caching layer needed).\n\n## Consequences (anticipated)"
}

{
  "command": "gh pr create --title \"feat(auth): DataQ PATs phase 1 — second authenticator behind the auth seam (REST + /mcp)\" --milestone \"v1.1 Week 1 — Snowflake close-out + PATs\" --body \"Fixes #461 — **ADR 0026 phase 1**: user-scoped personal access tokens (\\`dq_live_…\\`) as a **second authenticator behind \\`get_current_user\\`**, accepted identically by the REST API and \\`/mcp\\`. The first non-Azure impl on the identity seam (ADR 0010) — breaks the Azure-AD-only auth dependency while Azure AD is still live as the reference validator (the W1 point of pulling this forward).\n\n## What\n- **\\`api_keys\\` table** (migration \\`b0c1d2e3f4a5\\` — additive only, tested up/down/up locally): \\`user_id\\` FK **CASCADE** (keys die with the user), unique \\`key_hash\\`, mandatory \\`expires_at\\`, soft \\`revoked_at\\`, \\`last_used_at\\`.\n- **Service**: token = \\`dq_live_\\` + \\`secrets.token_urlsafe(32)\\`; **SHA-256 at rest** (indexed O(1) verification; deliberate deviation from the ADR stub's argon2/bcrypt — machine-generated ~256-bit secrets don't need a slow KDF, which would cost ~100ms+ *per request* and force an O(n) scan; GitHub/GitLab practice; full rationale in the ADR's phase-1 record); **uniform 401** for unknown/revoked/expired (no state oracle); expiry default 90d / max 365d, no non-expiring keys; prefix-only logging; \\`last_used_at\\` writes throttled to 60s.\n- **REST seam**: Azure scheme → \\`auto_error=False\\`; PAT branch first by prefix (disjoint — a PAT is never a valid JWT), Azure fallback intact; a bad \\`dq_live_\\` bearer 401s and never falls through — including in dev-bypass mode.\n- **MCP seam**: composite \\`_PatOrJwtVerifier\\` (PAT by prefix, else the same-coordinates Azure \\`JWTVerifier\\`); the PAT-resolved user id rides a DataQ-internal claim into \\`resolve_current_user\\` (fail-closed if the user vanished).\n- **Surface**: \\`POST/GET /api/v1/me/api-keys\\`, \\`DELETE /api/v1/me/api-keys/{id}\\` — show-once plaintext (creation response only), metadata-only list, idempotent owner-scoped revoke (cross-user → 404, indistinguishable from nonexistent).\n- **Docs**: new \\`docs/api-keys.md\\` guide (+ mkdocs nav), \\`mcp-setup.md\\` now recommends PATs over browser-token pasting, ADR 0026 flipped **Accepted (phase 1)** with the build record, \\`api_keys\\` added to the ER diagram.\n\n## Tests\n- Service battery: hash-at-rest, show-once, uniform-401 triple, throttling, owner cascade, cross-user isolation.\n- API end-to-end (TestClient, dev-bypass): PAT authenticates as its **owner** (not the bypass user), bad/revoked PATs 401, lifecycle-over-PAT-auth, expiry bounds 422.\n- Seam units: bearer/PAT parsing, PAT-without-Azure, no-credential 401, bad-PAT-never-falls-through(-even-with-valid-Azure), dev-bypass fail-closed.\n- MCP verifier units: valid PAT → AccessToken with the user claim, bad PAT → None, non-PAT bearer delegates to JWT, resolve fail-closed.\n- Full backend suite **1332 passed, coverage 98.4%**; Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit clean locally.\n\n## Post-merge (issue exit criterion)\nDeploy → mint **1 workspace-admin PAT** (as dataq-admin, short expiry) + **1 member PAT**, exercise both against live REST + \\`/mcp\\`, evidence on #461.\n\n## Migration checklist\n- Backward-compatible: additive table only, no existing-table changes. Rollback: \\`alembic downgrade -1\\` drops \\`api_keys\\` (tested locally up→down→up).\n\n🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)\"",

> AGENT

Everything for #613 is now in flight. Status while the reviews and CI run:

**dbt (your question, resolved):** dbt as a third `OrchestrationProvider` is exactly the right test of the ADR 0011 seam, and the hosting research settled the neutrality question — details in my earlier message and on the issues: **dbt Cloud's free Developer plan has no API access and no scheduler** (that starts at the $100/user/mo Starter plan), so the canonical hosted option is out; **dbt Projects on Snowflake** (GA Nov 2025) and **Databricks dbt job tasks** both run dbt fine but make the *observation channel* vendor-shaped — you'd be building a Snowflake-tasks or Databricks-Jobs provider with dbt incidental, and the Snowflake one dies with the trial. The neutral answer is to bind the provider to **dbt's own universal surface** — `run_results.json` artifacts + an `on-run-end` HMAC webhook (mirroring the Airflow callback + 10-min poll pattern we already have) — which works identically under a self-hosted container now, local compose after the wind-down, and even under the vendor hosts later. Filed as [#611](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/611) (the `DbtProvider`, W2), [#609](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/609) rescoped to self-hosted dbt Core, tracker PR #612 merged.

**#461 PATs — built and in review as [PR #613](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/613):**
- Full implementation: `api_keys` table (migration tested up/down/up), `dq_live_` tokens SHA-256-at-rest with uniform 401s, show-once mint/list/revoke at `/me/api-keys`, PAT branch in front of Azure on the REST seam (`auto_error=False`), and a PAT-or-JWT composite verifier on `/mcp`.
- 44 targeted tests + full backend suite **1332 passed at 98.4% coverage**; Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit clean. The one gate catch was the ER-diagram sync test — `api_keys` is now in [architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).
- ADR 0026 flipped to **Accepted (phase 1)** with the build record, including the deliberate SHA-256-vs-argon2 deviation rationale; new [docs/api-keys.md](docs/api-keys.md) user guide; tracker rows updated.
- Four review agents (code-reviewer, silent-failure-hunter, test-analyzer, migration-safety) and the 12-check CI gate are running now — I'll fix any findings in the PR, then squash-merge, deploy, and mint the admin PAT (as dataq-admin) + a member PAT live against REST and `/mcp`.

**Sources:** [dbt pricing](https://www.getdbt.com/pricing) · [dbt Cloud APIs overview](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/dbt-cloud-apis/overview) · [dbt Projects on Snowflake](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-engineering/dbt-projects-on-snowflake) · [scheduling dbt projects on Snowflake](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/data-engineering/dbt-projects-on-snowflake-schedule-project-execution)

I've completed a thorough review of PR #613. I verified every security-critical path against the actual code (not the PR description), checked the migration chain, timezone handling, the test DB backend (Postgres, not SQLite — so no naive/aware comparison trap), and the MCP verifier lifecycle.

## Verdict: no blockers, no should-fix defects survived verification.

The auth-seam implementation is correct and the security-critical behaviors hold up under scrutiny:

- **auto_error=False does not weaken JWT rejection.** In `_get_current_user_real` (backend/app/core/auth.py:169), an invalid/absent Azure token yields `azure_user is None` → explicit `DataQError(401)`. Scope/issuer/audience/expiry are still enforced inside the scheme (it returns `None` on any failure rather than skipping validation). No fallthrough.
- **PAT/JWT branches are genuinely disjoint.** `dq_live_`-prefixed tokens route to `resolve_token` and can never reach the Azure validator; a bad PAT raises a uniform 401 and never falls through to Azure (backend/app/core/auth.py:176-179). Confirmed by `test_get_current_user_real_bad_pat_never_falls_through_to_azure`.
- **Uniform-401 / no oracle.** `ApiKeyAuthError` is one message for unknown/revoked/expired (api_key_service.py:35-48), and the failure log records only `token[:12]` (the `dq_live_`+4 display prefix) for all three cases — no state-distinguishing oracle in responses or logs. Verified by `test_resolve_unknown_revoked_expired_all_uniform_401`.
- **No plaintext leakage.** Only the hash is stored; plaintext appears solely in the show-once `ApiKeyCreated.token`; logs carry `key_prefix` only.
- **Timezone handling correct.** `expires_at`/`revoked_at`/`last_used_at` are `DateTime(timezone=True)` in both model and migration; comparisons use `datetime.now(UTC)` (aware-vs-aware). Tests run on Postgres, so no naive/aware TypeError.
- **MCP SessionLocal lifecycle is sound.** `_PatOrJwtVerifier.verify_token` (backend/app/mcp/auth.py) opens `SessionLocal()`, resolves, and closes in `finally`; the resolved user id is carried via the internal `dataq_user_id` claim and re-loaded fail-closed in `resolve_current_user` (raises if the user vanished between verify and tool call). An Azure-signed token cannot forge that claim.
- **Migration is additive/backward-compatible.** New `api_keys` table only; `down_revision a9b0c1d2e3f4` is the real prior head (linear chain, verified); no existing-table change, no two-step needed.
- Test coverage is strong on failure modes: cross-user 404 isolation, revoke idempotency, expiry bounds (422), last_used throttle, MCP missing-user fail-closed.

## Observations (nits — not defects, no action required)

- **backend/app/api/v1/api_keys.py:56 — a PAT can mint further PATs.** Every `/me/api-keys` route only requires `get_current_user`, which a PAT satisfies, so a leaked key can mint sibling keys (up to 365-day expiry). Revoking the compromised key does not evict an attacker who already minted a sibling. This is a common accepted PAT tradeoff and consistent with ADR 0026's "inherits the owner's grants" framing, but it isn't called out as an accepted risk anywhere. Worth one line in the ADR's phase-1 record if you want it on the record; not a code change.
- **backend/app/services/api_key_service.py:151-153 — `resolve_token` commits the request-scoped `db` session mid-dependency** (the `last_used_at` write) before the route handler runs. Harmless here (nothing else is pending at auth time, and `get_db` rolls back cleanly on later errors), just slightly surprising that the auth dependency commits.
- `create_key` validates `expires_in_days` (api_key_service.py:88) redundantly with the Pydantic `ge/le` on `ApiKeyCreate` — intentional defense for direct/service callers, fine to keep.

Relevant files: /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/app/services/api_key_service.py, /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/app/core/auth.py, /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/app/mcp/auth.py, /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/app/api/v1/api_keys.py.

    kind: str = "expectation",
    warn_threshold: float | None = None,
    fail_threshold: float | None = None,
    critical_threshold: float | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Add a new check (a Great Expectations expectation) to a suite.

    Use this for 'add a null check on email to the customer suite'. ``name`` is a
    human label; ``expectation_type`` is a GX expectation (e.g.
    ``expect_column_values_to_not_be_null``); ``config`` carries its arguments
    (e.g. ``{"column": "email"}``). Optional warn/fail/critical thresholds band
    the result severity. Requires edit access. Returns the created check's id.
    """
    sid = _parse_uuid(suite_id, field="suite_id")
    _reject_nul(name=name, expectation_type=expectation_type, kind=kind, config=config or {})
    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
        require_permission(session, sid, user.id, minimum="edit")
        check = check_service.create_check(
            session,
            suite_id=sid,
            name=name,
            kind=kind,
            expectation_type=expectation_type,
            config=config or {},
            warn_threshold=Decimal(str(warn_threshold)) if warn_threshold is not None else None,
            fail_threshold=Decimal(str(fail_threshold)) if fail_threshold is not None else None,
            critical_threshold=(
                Decimal(str(critical_threshold)) if critical_threshold is not None else None
            ),
            actor_id=user.id,
        )
        return {
            "id": str(check.id),
            "suite_id": suite_id,
            "name": check.name,
            "expectation_type": check.expectation_type,
        }


@mcp.tool
def profile_column(
    suite_id: str,
    columns: list[str],
    table: str | None = None,
    schema: str | None = None,
    catalog: str | None = None,
    path: str | None = None,
    file_format: str | None = None,
    top_n: int = 10,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Profile one or more columns of a table or file on a suite's connection.

    Use this for 'profile the revenue column in FACT_ORDERS'. Runs the column
    profiler (no persistence) and returns, per column: null count + fraction,
    distinct count, min/max, and the top ``top_n`` values. Give ``table`` (+
    optional ``schema``/``catalog``) for a SQL datasource, or ``path`` (+
    ``file_format``) for a flat file. Requires edit access to the suite.
    """
    sid = _parse_uuid(suite_id, field="suite_id")
    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
        suite = require_permission(session, sid, user.id, minimum="edit")
        connection = session.get(Connection, suite.connection_id)
        if connection is None:
            raise ToolError("suite has no connection")
        result = profile_service.profile_connection(
            connection,
            columns=columns,
            top_n=top_n,
            table=table,
            schema=schema,
            catalog=catalog,
            path=path,
            file_format=file_format,
            secret_store=get_secret_store(),
        )
        return {
            "row_count": result.row_count,
            "table": result.table,
            "path": result.path,
            "columns": [
                {
                    "column": c.column,
                    "null_count": c.null_count,
                    "null_fraction": c.null_fraction,
                    "distinct_count": c.distinct_count,
                    "min_value": c.min_value,
                    "max_value": c.max_value,
                    "top_values": c.top_values,
                }
                for c in result.columns
            ],
        }


def build_mcp_app() -> Any:
    """Build the MCP ASGI app to mount at ``/mcp`` (``path='/'`` since we mount).

    Returns ``None`` when MCP must not be exposed (no resolvable auth — see
    ``auth.mcp_enabled``), so ``main.py`` skips the mount and the endpoint never
    goes live unauthenticated.
    """
    if not mcp_enabled():
        log.warning("mcp_disabled_no_auth", note="/mcp not mounted — no Azure auth or dev bypass")
        return None
    log.info(
        "mcp_enabled", auth="azure_ad" if get_settings().azure_auth_configured else "dev_bypass"
    )
    return mcp.http_app(path="/")

2	
3	A suite's `target` (#215) is a small JSONB document shaped like the column
4	profiler request (``table`` / ``schema`` / ``catalog`` / ``path`` /
5	``file_format``), datasource-typed. The `CheckRunner` interface is *table-shaped*
6	— for a flat-file datasource the file path rides the ``table`` argument
7	(``flatfile.py``) — so every datasource resolves to the same triple the worker
8	hands to ``run_service.execute_run`` and ``build_check_runner``:
9	
10	    snowflake      → table (+ schema)
11	    unity_catalog  → table (+ schema) + catalog        (catalog.schema.table)
12	    adls_gen2 / s3 → path  (carried as `table`; schema/catalog unused)
13	
14	A flat-file target can instead be a **batch** spec — files arrive in batches
15	(``orders_2026-06-01.csv`` …) and a run targets one of them: ``pattern`` (a regex
16	whose first capture group is the batch key) + ``strategy`` (``latest`` /
17	``specific``, with ``batch`` for ``specific``) + an optional ``prefix`` to list
18	under. The concrete path can only be known by *listing the store*, so it's
19	resolved at run time (`materialize_path`), not at save time.
20	
21	Resolution is two-phase so write-time validation stays pure (no network, no GX):
22	
23	* `resolve_target` (pure) validates the spec and returns the static triple plus,
24	  for a batch flat-file target, an unresolved `BatchSpec`. `validate_target` is
25	  the write-time wrapper `suite_service` calls, so a malformed/wrong-datasource
26	  target is a clean 422 at save.
27	* `materialize_path` (run-time, may touch the network) turns a `BatchSpec` into a
28	  concrete file path by listing + resolving the batch; for every other target it
29	  returns the already-resolved table. It raises `flatfile.BatchNotFoundError`
30	  when no file matches — the run path maps that to *skipped* results (the data
31	  hasn't landed yet), not a failure.
32	
33	FastAPI-free: takes a connection type + the stored dict, raises `DataQError`.

"""FastMCP server — 8 curated, LLM-facing tools over the DataQ service layer.

Mounted into FastAPI at ``/mcp`` (see ``main.py``). Every tool is a thin wrapper:
open a session → resolve the caller (same Azure AD token as the REST API) →
call the *same* service function with the *same* per-suite authz → return an
LLM-shaped dict. No business logic lives here.

All eight are registered as MCP **tools** (not resources): an LLM client invokes
tools from natural language, whereas resource-templates with required arguments
aren't reliably auto-called — and the acceptance bar is "Claude answers the
canonical NL queries" (ADR 0008). Docstrings are written for natural-language
selection, not REST consumers (CLAUDE.md §10).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import uuid
from collections.abc import Generator
from contextlib import contextmanager
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Any

from fastmcp import FastMCP
from fastmcp.exceptions import ToolError

from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from backend.app.api.v1._base import contains_nul
from backend.app.core.config import get_settings
from backend.app.core.errors import DataQError
from backend.app.core.logging import get_logger
from backend.app.core.secrets import get_secret_store
from backend.app.db.models import Check, Connection, Run, User
from backend.app.db.session import get_session
from backend.app.mcp.auth import (
    McpAuthError,
    build_auth_provider,
    mcp_enabled,
    resolve_current_user,
)
from backend.app.services import (
    check_service,
    dashboard_service,
    orchestration_service,
    profile_service,
    run_dispatch,
    run_service,
    run_target,
    suite_service,
)
from backend.app.services.suite_authz import require_permission

log = get_logger(__name__)

_INSTRUCTIONS = (
    "DataQ is a data-quality monitoring platform. These tools read and act on DQ "
    "suites (collections of checks), their runs and results, the overall health "
    "score, and orchestration (ADF/Airflow) pipeline status. Use them to answer "
    "questions like 'what failed today?', 'run the orders suite on DEV', 'why did "
    "the customer pipeline fail?', or 'add a null check on email'."

    assert out["columns"][0]["column"] == "revenue"
    assert out["columns"][0]["null_count"] == 2

def _user(db_session: Any, email: str = "ada@acme.io") -> User:
    u = User(aad_object_id=uuid.uuid4().hex, email=email)
    db_session.add(u)
    db_session.flush()
    return u


def _suite(db_session: Any, owner: User, *, with_target: bool = True) -> Suite:
    conn = Connection(
        name=f"sf-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}",
        type="snowflake",
        env="dev",
        config={"account": "a", "schema": "PUBLIC"},
        secret_ref="kv-sf",
        created_by=owner.id,
    )
    db_session.add(conn)
    db_session.flush()
    suite = Suite(
        name="Orders",
        connection_id=conn.id,
        created_by=owner.id,
        target={"table": "ORDERS"} if with_target else None,
    )
    db_session.add(suite)
    db_session.commit()
    return suite


def _as(monkeypatch: Any, db_session: Any, user: User) -> None:
    """Run the next tool call as ``user`` against the test session."""
    monkeypatch.setattr(server, "get_session", lambda: db_session)
    monkeypatch.setattr(db_session, "close", lambda: None)
    monkeypatch.setattr(server, "resolve_current_user", lambda _session: user)


def test_list_suites_shapes_each_accessible_suite(db_session: Any, monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    user = _user(db_session)
    suite = _suite(db_session, user)
    db_session.add(Check(suite_id=suite.id, name="c", expectation_type="expect_x", config={}))
    db_session.commit()
    _as(monkeypatch, db_session, user)

    out = server.list_suites()
    assert len(out) == 1
    assert out[0]["name"] == "Orders"
    assert out[0]["datasource"] == "snowflake"
    assert out[0]["env"] == "dev"
    assert out[0]["check_count"] == 1
    assert out[0]["last_run"] is None


def test_get_suite_results_returns_latest_run_per_check(db_session: Any, monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    user = _user(db_session)
    suite = _suite(db_session, user)
    check = Check(suite_id=suite.id, name="not null email", expectation_type="expect_x", config={})
    db_session.add(check)
    run = Run(suite_id=suite.id, status="succeeded")
    db_session.add(run)
    db_session.flush()
    db_session.add(Result(run_id=run.id, check_id=check.id, status="fail"))
    db_session.commit()
    _as(monkeypatch, db_session, user)

    out = server.get_suite_results(str(suite.id))
    assert out["run"]["status"] == "succeeded"
    assert out["checks"][0]["name"] == "not null email"
    assert out["checks"][0]["status"] == "fail"
```

That lane stores Olivia's OIDC browser session; I can drive a quick Playwright pass (or use its refresh token) to get her access token, hit `POST /api/v1/me/api-keys` with it, and never touch your az login. PATs are strictly self-service (`/me`), so the admin can't mint on her behalf — I need *some* bearer that is Olivia, and the captured session is the least disruptive source.

**Plan B (only if the captured session is stale beyond renewal): yes, an az login as Olivia.** The Azure CLI is pre-authorized on the API scope (#565), so `az account get-access-token --resource api://214911…` mints her bearer non-interactively once she's signed in. Two ways to do it without losing your current session:

- or run the Olivia login under a separate `AZURE_CONFIG_DIR` (device-code flow) so your dataq-admin login is untouched.

So: nothing needed from you right now on the Olivia front — the sequence is deploy → admin PAT (az as dataq-admin, already in place) → Olivia PAT via the captured session, and I'll only come back to you if that session won't renew. // WebStorageStateStore) — Playwright's built-in storageState can't capture it.
//
// The captured token expires like any AAD token (~1h); the file is reused
// while fresh and re-captured otherwise.

// cwd-relative (pnpm runs from frontend/): __dirname doesn't exist under ESM.
export const SESSION_FILE = path.resolve('e2e-live', '.auth', 'session.json');
const MAX_AGE_MS = 40 * 60 * 1000; // re-login when the capture is older than 40 min

export default async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  const liveBaseURL = process.env.E2E_LIVE_BASE_URL;
  if (!liveBaseURL) {
    throw new Error('live-smoke lane requires E2E_LIVE_BASE_URL');
  }
  // Stat-and-use (no exists pre-check — CodeQL js/file-system-race): a missing
  // file just means "no capture yet".
  let capturedAtMs = 0;
  try {
    capturedAtMs = fs.statSync(SESSION_FILE).mtimeMs;
  } catch {
    // no session captured yet
  }
  if (capturedAtMs && Date.now() - capturedAtMs < MAX_AGE_MS) {
    return; // fresh enough — reuse
  }

  const browser = await chromium.launch({ headless: false });
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto(liveBaseURL);
  console.log('\n[live-smoke] Complete the sign-in in the opened browser…');
  // The post-login landing is the Dashboard; give MFA up to 5 minutes.
  await page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard', level: 3 }).waitFor({ timeout: 300_000 });
  const session: string = await page.evaluate(() => JSON.stringify({ ...sessionStorage }));
  fs.mkdirSync(path.dirname(SESSION_FILE), { recursive: true });
  // Temp-write + rename: atomic replace, and no write decision hangs off the
  // earlier stat (a parallel capture just loses the rename race harmlessly).
  const tmp = `${SESSION_FILE}.${process.pid}.tmp`;
  fs.writeFileSync(tmp, session);
  fs.renameSync(tmp, SESSION_FILE);
  await browser.close();
  console.log('[live-smoke] Session captured.');
}
```
